newsitem.title: USA: Wall St. open depends on data, budget deal a bonus.
newsitem.headline: Wall St. open depends on data, budget deal a bonus.

text.p: Wall Street stocks should take early direction from the second quarter employment cost index data on Tuesday, alert to any signs of wage inflation which might trigger fears of a rate hike, analysts said.
But markets would be underpinned by a historic accord between President Clinton and U.S. Republican leaders to balance the federal budget and cut taxes, they said.
"All eyes are going to be watching the ECI (employment cost index)," Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments said.

"But you also have the budget deal, which is giving a boost to the bond market," he said. "If the ECI comes in as expected, showing subdued inflation, it could spark a strong rally in the bond market which would carry over to stocks."
The employment cost index, due out at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, was forecast to rise 0.8 percent in the second quarter compared to a 0.6 percent gain in the previous quarter.
Analysts have said Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan pays close attention to this figure, for signs of upward pressure on wages and benefits.
But unless the employment cost index were surprising strong, stocks could be boosted by the announcement of a pact between Clinton and the Republicans to balance the budget.
The historic agreement would aim to balance the budget for the first time since 1969 and cut taxes by $90 billion over the next five years.

"The budget deal is a huge bonus," Robert Froelich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds, said. "It could bring a little more focus to cyclical stocks, because to keep a balanced budget in place, the economy has to remain strong."

In London trading, shares of Philip Morris Cos Inc gained on a favorable response to the accord. A Republican source said U.S. cigarette taxes will increase by up to $0.15 per pact over the next five years.
Tech stocks could also regain some ground on Tuesday, after lagging the broader market yesterday, Cardillo said.
In early trade, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index gained 0.35 points. The long bond added 3/32 to 6.40 percent.
On Monday, the Dow industrials finished up 7.67 points to 8,121.11. The Nasdaq composite lost 6.05 points to 1563.53.

The dollar fell against the yen in Tokyo amid heavy sales by Japanese exporters and profit-takers. It was trading at 117.45/50 yen. In Europe, the dollar was near session lows, trading at 1.8344/54 marks.
Japan's Nikkei average closed off 172.52 points, or 0.84 percent, at 20,402.74.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 20.8 at 4883.4.
U.S. stocks were mixed to slightly firmer in London trading, with some sectors benefitting from the new U.S. budget and tax deal.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that some Wall Street firms offer funds that have issued preferred stock offering dividends that get favorable tax treatment as capital gains.

The New York Times said in its Market Place column that Donna Karan appointed John Idol, an executive from Polo Ralph Lauren Corp as chief executive of her troubled company, enabling her to focus on her strength -- designing clothes.
